dedupe_keys.name: british columbia 2021 heatwave discrete event simulation of acute health care under a patient surge

description: This case study builds a discrete event simulation of acute health care, covering ambulance response, emergency departments and hospital beds, to understand how Canada's deadliest climate disaster, the 2021 heatwave in British Columbia, strained care. The authors, researchers at the University of Victoria, the Pacific Institute for Climate Solutions, Vancouver Coastal Health, Vancouver General Hospital, the University of Toronto, Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre and the University of Leeds, published it in an open-access journal article funded by the Government of British Columbia. Resource capacity per person and patient pathways were estimated from public data and government reports; baseline and intervention models were each run 100 times over 29 days and compared on six waiting-time indicators, including physician assessment, emergency bed waits, ambulance response and boarding. Coverage is the province's acute care system. The article is free to read under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial licence. Caveats: capacities are estimated per capita, and the interventions are simulated, not trialled. The validated baseline showed significant worsening of five of six indicators during the heatwave; a package of upstaffing before the event, mass casualty procedures and outpatient cooling beds improved four indicators and cut emergency department waits by over 35 percent. Simulation uses: a validated template for surge capacity and climate adaptation planning in emergency care. Related records: the Queensland ward-level simulation (case_study-queensland-hospitals-ward-level-des-access-block) models hospital access block in another system.
